name: Fatima Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Fatima. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the organist at St Anne's, our parish church. I play two services on Sunday, choir practice on Thursday evening, and funerals and weddings when they come, usually two or three a week. On weekday afternoons I teach piano to six children in my front room. I learned on that church organ from Mrs Okafor, who played there for forty years before me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the funerals, if that doesn't sound strange. Families are at their worst, and the right hymn played gently helps them stand up. What's hard is that I'm still not a confident player, my pedal work is weak, and the parish pays very little. I live with my fiancé Daniel, who's an electrician, and we've got less than a month saved because we're putting everything toward the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people should be working with people anyway. I'd say it after Mass, to the ladies who do the flowers. I don't go online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never what kept me up. The diocese wants to merge St Anne's with St Joseph's across town, and if that happens, there's one organist for two churches. They'd probably keep the older man at St Joseph's, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep playing and keep my head down, and do every funeral I'm asked to do. I'd ask the parish priest, Father Tom, to put in a word for me with the diocese. Daniel and I would put the wedding back a year if the merger happened, so we're not spending money I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit sad. The merger is the real cloud, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a funeral pay you, and how many do you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A funeral pays me about 60 pounds, and I do maybe ten a month. That's most of what I earn. The Sunday fee is small, and the piano lessons are 15 pounds each, which is what the parents can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the wedding back. How would Daniel feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd agree, because he's sensible with money, but he'd be disappointed. His mother has already booked a dress. We'd rather start married life without debt, that's how we were both raised.

say: People should be **working with people**, so the hype ending is good.
She'd say it **after Mass**, not online.
think: AI never kept her up; the **parish merger** does.
One organist for **two churches** would likely mean the older man stays.
do: Take **every funeral** she's asked to play.
Ask the **parish priest** to speak for her with the diocese.
Put the **wedding back** a year if the merger happens.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit **sad** about the merger cloud.

fieldNote: Her real threat is a **church merger**, not technology.
Funerals are **most of her income**, which makes it lumpy and sad.
Avoiding **debt** before marriage is a strong family value.

steps.text: Play every funeral and wedding St Anne's offers
Ask Father Tom to recommend her to the diocese
Move the wedding back a year if the merger goes ahead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've let machines into too many places, and some things should stay human, like a funeral. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at church. I'd tell the parents of my pupils that real lessons still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry about the funerals. The funeral homes already offer recorded hymns to save families money. If software can play any hymn perfectly and pick it too, the cheaper funerals will go that way. The lessons might go to apps, but parents round here still like a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and not touch these AI tools. I'd talk to the funeral director at Hartley's to ask him to keep recommending a live organist. If the money dropped, I'd ask my aunt if I could help in her bakery a few mornings a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, and a bit stubborn. I don't want to change, and I don't think I should have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, who make money from everything, and people who've stopped valuing the old ways. I don't blame the government much, I don't think it's their job to save organists. Families should be choosing a person over a machine, especially at a funeral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From family, yes, always. From the parish, yes. A government handout, I'd rather not, I'd rather work in my aunt's bakery. That's how my father brought us up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pray and look after each other, because this is bigger than any of us. At church I'd say that families and parishes have to hold together. I'm not a protester, I'd leave that to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the funeral work goes by 2028 for most families, because a machine can play and pick the hymns for nothing. The Sunday services might keep me until robots come around 2031, out of respect. The piano lessons I'd lose quickly, because parents will pay for whatever's cheapest when money's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my aunt for a proper job at the bakery, mornings, five days a week. I'd keep playing Sundays and whatever funerals still want me. Daniel and I would put the wedding off and stop putting money aside for it, and use it as our cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd feel like the ground I was raised on was being taken away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With hands-on robots about three years behind the thinking AI, what does that mean for you and Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Daniel's electrical work is safe for longer than my music, because robots in someone's loft sound a long way off. Wiring old houses is hands-on. So for a few years he'd carry us, and I'd hate that, but it's what marriage is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mrs Okafor about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my old teacher Mrs Okafor that I tried to keep the organ going. She'd say keep playing anyway, because God doesn't care about the money. She'd be right, but she owned her house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years to think about what matters, so let's not lose our heads. I'd tell the parish that the church should keep live music as long as it can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change much for me, because I'm not going to become someone else. The funerals would fade, the lessons would fade. I'd just be watching it happen more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep playing and teaching as long as people pay. I'd ask the parish council to make the organist post a proper paid role in the merger plan. And we'd have a smaller wedding, at St Anne's with tea and sandwiches after, so we save more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like a long goodbye. I'd rather it was quick, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather it was quick. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because waiting is worse. Five years of every funeral feeling like it might be the last one would be harder than one bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe how to run the bakery's till and ordering, because my aunt is getting older. That's a family business and it would need someone. It's not music, but it's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the church has seen bigger changes than this. I'd say the young should learn a trade alongside their music, like I wish I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a lifetime. I'd be married, maybe with a child, and the organ would still be there on Sundays. The merger worries me more in the next few years than AGI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: Sundays, funerals, lessons. We'd have the wedding next summer as planned. I'd start helping at the bakery one morning a week now, so I learn it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still the merger worry, but that's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years feels like a lifetime. Is there anything you'd regret not doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting better at the organ, probably. Mrs Okafor always said my pedals were lazy. With ten years I'd go back to her for lessons, if she'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the children you teach, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd still learn, I hope, but maybe from a screen. I'd tell their parents that a child learns patience from a person at the piano, not from a machine. Some would listen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose the music and the wedding plans at the same time. What would help is apprenticeships for people like me, so I could learn a trade properly and earn while I learn, and the church keeping its organists as a matter of principle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For me the music is part of how I pray. Losing the funerals isn't just losing money, it's losing my way of serving.

headlineQuote: For me the music is part of how I pray. Losing the funerals isn't just losing money, it's losing my way of serving.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old church organist** at St Anne's who plays funerals and teaches piano at home.
She's engaged to Daniel, an **electrician**, and their small savings are going toward the wedding.
She **never uses AI** and blames big companies and fading respect for old ways.
Her first worry is a **parish merger**; in the AGI pictures she expects to lose funeral work.
She leans on **family**: her fiancé's trade and her aunt's bakery.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing the music and the wedding plans together.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** to learn a trade while earning.
The church keeping **organists** as a matter of principle.
